title: The Five Elements
paragraphs: > A structured blend of > Earth, fire, water, air and space > As the world is, > The use words are made of > Must be undistorted, > Undeviating from the norms > That go with the classifications of > The human -- non-human generic distinction, > And the five genders thereof.

By way of interpreting this verse, Iḷampūraṇar observes that the world is composed of the five elements, viz., earth, fire, water, air and space. He then goes on to explain the two words in the verse kalattal and mayakkam. The former is a mix, as of pearl, coral, sapphire and ruby. The latter signifies the one like the melted blend of gold, silver and copper.

The world, therefore, exists at two levels - one as a mixture, and the other as an undifferentiated one made up of the five elements, which the compound term in the verse kalanta mayakkam signifies. Thus goes the explanation of the commentator.
Now, what does the expression in Tamil kiṇaṟu veṭṭap pūtam puṟappaṭṭatu (the elements surfaced as the well was dug) mean?

As one digs up the well, the ‘earth’ piles up - one element. The ‘air’ shut up in the earth comes out - second element The ‘water’ gushes forth - third element The ‘sky’ is reflected in the water - fourth element The sun’s ‘fire’ purifies the water - fifth element.

Thus remains the world as the structured fusion of the elements. The phenomena of the world must therefore be denoted without deviation from the norms of usage, and in terms of the human--non-human generic distinction and the five genders informing them.

Violation of the norms of usage would result in distortion and variation of meanings of words. The things of the world must be represented without deviation from the established conventions and in accord with human--non-human classification and gender distinction. Thus goes the import of the Tolkāppiyam verse.
Pērāciriyar’s explanation is that the five elements remain individual entities and at the same time they remain fused with the things of the world.
